title: Reproductive Organs & Special Senses
summary: Study the reproductive organs, the eye and the inner ear, where highly specialized cells do remarkable work.

lessons.title: Testis, Spermatogenesis & Male Ducts

levels.kid:
Inside the testis are hundreds of tiny, twisty tubes, packed like spaghetti in a bowl. These tubes are factories that make sperm, the cells that carry half of a dad's instructions to make a baby.

The factory works like an assembly line. Round starter cells sit at the outside edge of each tube. As they grow up, they move toward the middle. By the end, each one has a head and a long swimming tail.

Big helper cells called **Sertoli cells** act like nannies. They feed the young sperm and protect them.

The new sperm cannot swim well yet. They travel through a long, coiled tube called the **epididymis**, where they finish growing up, a bit like waiting rooms that turn beginners into strong swimmers.
levels.hs:
The **testis** is the male gonad. Under a microscope, most of it is made of **seminiferous tubules**, coiled tubes where sperm are produced. This process is called **spermatogenesis**.

Inside each tubule, cells are arranged from the outside in by age:
- **Spermatogonia**: stem cells on the basement membrane that divide by mitosis.
- **Primary spermatocytes**: cells that enter **meiosis**, the special division that halves the chromosome number.
- **Spermatids**: small round cells that result from meiosis.
- **Spermatozoa**: mature sperm near the central space (lumen), with a head and tail.

Tall **Sertoli cells** stretch from the edge to the lumen. They support developing sperm and form the **blood-testis barrier**, which protects the cells from the immune system. Between tubules, **Leydig cells** make **testosterone**.

The whole process takes roughly 64 to 74 days in humans. Sperm then leave through a series of ducts: the rete testis, efferent ductules, **epididymis**, and **vas deferens**. In the epididymis, sperm gain the ability to swim forward.

Real example: men who get mumps after puberty can develop orchitis, inflammation of the testis, which can damage seminiferous tubules and reduce fertility.
levels.college:
**Organization.** The testis is wrapped in a thick capsule, the **tunica albuginea**, and divided into about 250 lobules, each holding 1 to 4 highly coiled **seminiferous tubules**. Each tubule is lined by a **seminiferous (germinal) epithelium**, a stratified layer of germ cells supported by Sertoli cells. Outside it lie flattened, contractile **peritubular myoid cells**.

**Spermatogenesis** has three phases:
- **Spermatocytogenesis**: type A spermatogonia self-renew. Type B spermatogonia commit and become primary spermatocytes.
- **Meiosis**: primary spermatocytes (with their long prophase, the most common cells in sections) complete meiosis I to form secondary spermatocytes. These are rarely seen because they divide again quickly, producing haploid spermatids.
- **Spermiogenesis**: spermatids remodel without dividing. They form the **acrosome** (from the Golgi), condense the nucleus, grow a flagellum, and shed excess cytoplasm as residual bodies, which Sertoli cells phagocytose.

Germ cells remain linked by **cytoplasmic bridges** because cytokinesis is incomplete, so whole groups develop in sync.

**Sertoli cells** are joined near the base by tight junctions that create the **blood-testis barrier**. This barrier divides the epithelium into a basal compartment (spermatogonia) and an adluminal compartment (meiotic and later cells, which carry new antigens). Sertoli cells secrete **androgen-binding protein**, inhibin and tubular fluid.

**Leydig cells** in the interstitium are eosinophilic, lipid-rich steroid cells. Some contain crystals of Reinke.

**Hormonal control:** LH acts on Leydig cells to make testosterone. FSH and testosterone act on Sertoli cells.

**Duct epithelia**:
- Tubuli recti and rete testis: simple cuboidal.
- Efferent ductules: alternating ciliated and nonciliated cells, giving a scalloped lumen.
- Epididymis: pseudostratified columnar with **stereocilia** (long microvilli).
- Vas deferens: thick three-layered smooth muscle around a small lumen.
levels.phd:
**The cycle and the wave.** Clermont's classic work defined the **cycle of the seminiferous epithelium**: fixed cellular associations (stages) recur at any point along a tubule. Rodents show 12 stages (mouse) or 14 (rat) arranged as a longitudinal wave. In human tubules, stages form helical or patchy mosaics, and six stages are classically described. One human cycle lasts about 16 days, and roughly 4.5 cycles make up spermatogenesis. This explains the classic 64 to 74 day figure, derived by Heller and Clermont using tritiated thymidine labeling.

**Stem cell models.** In rodents, the A-single (As) model holds that single type A spermatogonia are the stem cells. These produce A-paired and A-aligned chains connected by bridges. Live imaging (Yoshida, Nakagawa) showed that chains can fragment and revert to stem function, and that GFRα1+ cells occupy niches near vasculature and interstitium. Niche maintenance depends on Sertoli **GDNF** and FGFs. In humans, the stem cells are classified as A-dark (reserve) and A-pale (active), although single-cell RNA-seq maps (e.g., Guo et al., 2018) now describe a continuum of states rather than two sharply separate types.

**Meiotic checkpoints.** The pachytene checkpoint and **meiotic sex chromosome inactivation** (MSCI) remove spermatocytes that synapse abnormally. Failure at this point leads to stage-specific apoptosis, which accounts for much of the physiological germ-cell loss.

**Barrier biology.** The blood-testis barrier is unusual. It sits near the basement membrane, combines tight junctions (claudin-11, occludin) with ectoplasmic specializations, and must open and reseal as preleptotene spermatocytes cross it. Cheng and Mruk's work implicates TGF-β3, TNFα and laminin fragments in coordinating this remodeling. Immune privilege also depends on Sertoli-derived immunomodulators and Treg-favoring signals, so it cannot be explained by physical sealing alone.

**Epididymal maturation.** Sperm acquire progressive motility and fertilizing capacity in transit. Changes include protein transfer by **epididymosomes**, disulfide crosslinking of the nucleus and tail, and membrane remodeling. Capacitation itself occurs later, in the female tract.
levels.expert:
**Testicular biopsy and histological patterns.** Male infertility workup relies on standardized descriptors:
- **Normal spermatogenesis** with obstruction: suggests a reconstructable blockage, such as vasal or epididymal obstruction.
- **Hypospermatogenesis**: all cell types present but reduced in number.
- **Maturation arrest**: development stops at a stage, often the spermatocyte stage.
- **Sertoli cell-only syndrome** (germ cell aplasia): tubules lined by Sertoli cells alone.
- **Tubular sclerosis/hyalinization**: as in Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), with Leydig cell clusters.

Scoring systems (Johnsen score, 1 to 10) remain in use, but patterns are often focal. Microdissection TESE (Schlegel) exploits this patchiness: an operating microscope identifies dilated, opaque tubules most likely to contain sperm in non-obstructive azoospermia. Genetic testing, including Y-chromosome AZFa/b/c microdeletions, changes predicted retrieval success. Complete AZFa or AZFb deletions predict very poor yield.

**Pharmacology.** Exogenous testosterone and anabolic androgens suppress LH and FSH through negative feedback. This collapses intratesticular testosterone, which normally exceeds serum levels many-fold, and can produce reversible azoospermia, a common iatrogenic cause seen in clinics. Gonadotoxic chemotherapy (alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide) targets dividing spermatogonia. Sperm banking before treatment, and experimental cryopreservation of prepubertal testicular tissue, address this risk. Male contraceptive research targets this biology: the nonhormonal retinoic-acid-receptor-α antagonist YCT529 and soluble adenylyl cyclase inhibitors exploit germ-cell-specific pathways.

**Oncology.** Germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) lines tubules with large, clear, atypical cells positive for OCT3/4 and PLAP. It precedes most postpubertal seminomas and nonseminomas, likely originating from fetal gonocytes that failed to mature. Spermatocytic tumour, by contrast, arises without GCNIS in older men.

**Pitfalls.** Testicular tissue fixed in formalin shrinks and distorts germ cells. Bouin's or Davidson's fixative preserves nuclear detail better for staging. Torsion and ischemia produce rapid germ cell loss that can mimic arrest.

**Open questions.** Can human spermatogonial stem cell transplantation or in vitro spermatogenesis restore fertility? Organotypic culture has produced sperm in mice (Sato and Ogawa), but complete human in vitro spermatogenesis remains unconfirmed.

keyPoints: Seminiferous tubules contain germ cells maturing from the basement membrane toward the lumen
Sequence: spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa
Sertoli cell tight junctions form the blood-testis barrier
Leydig cells in the interstitium make testosterone under LH control
Spermiogenesis remodels spermatids without cell division
Sperm gain motility while passing through the epididymis

test.q: Which cells in the testis produce testosterone?
test.explain: Leydig cells in the interstitium make testosterone in response to LH. Sertoli cells support germ cells instead.

test.q: Where are spermatogonia located within a seminiferous tubule?
test.explain: Spermatogonia are stem cells resting on the basement membrane, in the basal compartment.

test.q: What forms the blood-testis barrier?
test.explain: Tight junctions near the base of adjacent Sertoli cells separate the basal and adluminal compartments.

test.q: Spermiogenesis is best described as:
choices: Release of sperm into the epididymis
test.explain: In spermiogenesis, spermatids form an acrosome and flagellum and condense the nucleus, without dividing.

test.q: Why are secondary spermatocytes rarely seen in sections?
choices: They lack nuclei and stain poorly
They migrate out of the testis
They are destroyed by immune cells
test.explain: Secondary spermatocytes complete meiosis II rapidly, so few are caught in any one section.

test.q: The epididymis is lined by which epithelium?
test.explain: The epididymis has pseudostratified columnar epithelium bearing stereocilia, which are long microvilli.

test.q: Which duct has a scalloped lumen from alternating ciliated and nonciliated cells?
test.explain: Efferent ductules alternate tall ciliated and short nonciliated cells, producing a scalloped outline.

test.q: Why do groups of germ cells develop in sync?
choices: They share one Sertoli cell nucleus
They are linked by cytoplasmic bridges
They are clones made by meiosis
test.explain: Incomplete cytokinesis leaves cytoplasmic bridges connecting germ cells, which coordinates their development.

test.q: The vas deferens is recognized by its:
choices: Wide lumen lined by cuboidal cells
Network of channels in connective tissue
test.explain: The vas deferens has a small lumen surrounded by a thick wall of three smooth muscle layers.

test.q: What cap-like structure, made by the Golgi, covers the sperm head?
test.explain: The acrosome contains enzymes needed for fertilization and forms during spermiogenesis.

test.q: Primary spermatocytes undergo ___ to halve their chromosome number.
test.explain: Meiosis produces haploid spermatids from diploid spermatocytes.

test.q: Which pituitary hormone stimulates Leydig cells?
test.explain: LH (luteinizing hormone) drives testosterone production, while FSH acts on Sertoli cells.

kidTest.q: What do the tiny tubes in the testis make?
kidTest.explain: The twisty tubes are factories that make sperm.

kidTest.q: Where do the starter cells sit in each tube?
kidTest.explain: Starter cells sit at the edge and move toward the middle as they grow.

kidTest.q: What do Sertoli cells do?
kidTest.explain: Sertoli cells are like nannies that feed and protect developing sperm.

kidTest.q: What helps a sperm swim?
kidTest.explain: The long tail moves the sperm forward.

kidTest.q: Sperm finish growing up in a coiled tube called the e _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The epididymis is where sperm become strong swimmers.

advancedTest.q: Why must the blood-testis barrier exclude meiotic and later germ cells from the circulation?
choices: They secrete testosterone that would leak into the bloodstream
They need higher oxygen levels than plasma supplies
They require androgen-binding protein that is made by Leydig cells
They express new antigens that arise after immune tolerance forms
advancedTest.explain: Germ cells appearing after puberty carry antigens the immune system never learned to tolerate, so the adluminal compartment is sheltered.

advancedTest.q: A man using exogenous androgens develops azoospermia. The best mechanism is:
choices: Direct toxicity of androgens to spermatids
Androgen-driven obstruction of the efferent ductules
Excess inhibin causing Sertoli cell apoptosis
Suppressed LH and FSH lowering intratesticular testosterone
advancedTest.explain: Negative feedback reduces gonadotropins, and intratesticular testosterone collapses even though serum levels look high.

advancedTest.q: Why does microdissection TESE work in non-obstructive azoospermia?
choices: The surgery stimulates dormant stem cells to resume meiosis
Removing Leydig cells raises local FSH and restores production
Spermatogenesis is typically focal, so some tubules still make sperm
Sperm accumulate in the rete testis behind the obstruction
advancedTest.explain: Patterns such as Sertoli cell-only are often patchy, and dilated tubules visible under magnification are more likely to contain sperm.

advancedTest.q: Live-imaging of rodent spermatogonia challenged the strict A-single model by showing that:
choices: Stem cells sit in the lumen far from the vasculature
Connected spermatogonial chains can fragment and regain stem function
Sertoli cells can dedifferentiate to give rise to new spermatogonia
Spermatogonia divide by meiosis without cytoplasmic bridges
advancedTest.explain: Fragmentation of A-paired and A-aligned chains back into stem-like cells showed that stemness is more flexible than the As model proposed.

lessons.title: Ovary & Follicle Development

levels.kid:
Inside a girl's body are two small organs called **ovaries**. Each one is about the size of an almond. They hold tiny egg cells, each tucked inside a little bubble called a **follicle**.

Think of a follicle like a nest that grows around a baby bird. At first the nest is tiny and flat. Over time, helper cells pile up around the egg, and a pocket of fluid forms. The nest gets bigger and bigger.

About once a month, after puberty, one big follicle pops open and lets its egg out. Scientists call that **ovulation**. The leftover nest turns yellow and makes special messages called hormones.

A girl is born with all her eggs already inside. Most of them never get used.
levels.hs:
The **ovary** is the female gonad. It has two jobs: making egg cells (**oocytes**) and making hormones like **estrogen** and **progesterone**.

Under the microscope, the ovary has an outer **cortex**, packed with follicles, and an inner **medulla** full of blood vessels. The surface is covered by a single layer of cells, which is confusingly called the "germinal epithelium." Just under it lies a tough layer called the **tunica albuginea**.

A **follicle** is an oocyte plus the support cells around it. Follicles mature in stages:
- **Primordial follicle**: an oocyte wrapped in one layer of flat cells.
- **Primary follicle**: the support cells (**granulosa cells**) become cube-shaped and multiply. A clear coat, the **zona pellucida**, forms around the egg.
- **Secondary follicle**: fluid pockets appear between granulosa cells.
- **Mature (Graafian) follicle**: one big fluid-filled space, the **antrum**, with the egg sitting on a stalk of cells.

At ovulation the Graafian follicle bursts and releases the egg. What's left becomes the **corpus luteum** ("yellow body"), which makes progesterone. If no pregnancy happens, it shrinks into a white scar, the **corpus albicans**.

A newborn girl has roughly 1 to 2 million follicles. About 400 are ever ovulated. Most of the rest die by a process called **atresia**.
levels.college:
**Ovarian organization.** The ovary is covered by simple cuboidal **surface epithelium** (a modified mesothelium, misnamed germinal epithelium), above a dense connective **tunica albuginea**. The **cortex** contains follicles embedded in a highly cellular, fibroblast-rich stroma. The **medulla** holds loose connective tissue and large spiral vessels entering at the hilum.

**Folliculogenesis.**
- **Primordial**: a primary oocyte arrested in **prophase I** (diplotene), surrounded by a single layer of squamous pregranulosa cells. This is the resting reserve.
- **Primary**: granulosa cells become cuboidal. Multilayering forms the stratified granulosa. The **zona pellucida** (glycoproteins ZP1 to ZP4) appears, and gap junctions link oocyte and granulosa processes across it. Stromal cells organize into **theca**.
- **Secondary (antral)**: fluid-filled spaces (**Call-Exner bodies**, liquor folliculi) coalesce. The theca splits into a vascular, steroidogenic **theca interna** and a fibrous **theca externa**.
- **Graafian**: a single large **antrum**. The oocyte sits in the **cumulus oophorus**. The granulosa cells hugging the zona form the **corona radiata**.

**Two-cell, two-gonadotropin model.** LH drives theca interna cells to make androgens (androstenedione). These diffuse to granulosa cells, where FSH-induced **aromatase** (CYP19A1) converts them to estradiol.

**Ovulation.** The LH surge restarts meiosis. The oocyte completes meiosis I, extrudes the first polar body, and arrests at **metaphase II** until fertilization. The cumulus expands, proteases weaken the follicle wall at the stigma, and the follicle ruptures.

**Corpus luteum.** Granulosa cells become large pale **granulosa lutein cells**, which make progesterone. Theca cells become smaller, darker **theca lutein cells**, which make androgens. If pregnancy occurs, hCG rescues the corpus luteum. Otherwise it involutes into the hyalinized **corpus albicans**.

**Atresia** removes over 99% of follicles. Its histologic signs include pyknotic granulosa cells, a collapsed, folded zona, and the eventual glassy membrane.
levels.phd:
**Recruitment and dormancy.** Primordial follicles form perinatally as germ-cell nests break down. Their dormancy is actively maintained. Oocyte **PTEN** and **FOXO3** restrain the PI3K/AKT pathway. Castrillon and colleagues' Foxo3 knockout and Reddy and colleagues' oocyte-specific Pten deletion (2008) both caused global primordial activation and premature ovarian insufficiency. **mTORC1** in pregranulosa cells drives KIT ligand secretion, which activates oocyte **KIT** receptors. **AMH**, made by growing follicles, provides negative feedback on recruitment.

**Oocyte–somatic dialogue.** Growth is bidirectional. Oocyte-secreted **GDF9** and **BMP15** (TGF-β family members) drive granulosa proliferation and cumulus identity. Gdf9-null mice arrest at the primary stage (Dong and colleagues, 1996). Transzonal projections and connexin-37 gap junctions (with Cx43 between granulosa cells) deliver metabolites and **cGMP** to the oocyte. Granulosa cells make **CNP (NPPC)**, which acts on NPR2 in cumulus cells to generate cGMP. cGMP inhibits oocyte PDE3A, which keeps cAMP and PKA high and holds meiotic arrest.

**Meiotic resumption.** The LH receptor sits on mural granulosa and theca cells, not the oocyte. The LH surge induces EGF-like ligands (amphiregulin, epiregulin), lowers NPPC/NPR2 signalling, and closes gap junctions. Oocyte cGMP falls, PDE3A activates, cAMP drops, and CDK1/cyclin B (MPF) activity rises. The result is germinal vesicle breakdown. Cumulus expansion depends on hyaluronan synthase 2 and the stabilizers TSG6 and PTX3.

**Selection and dominance.** Antral follicles become FSH-dependent. The follicle that acquires granulosa LH receptors and the greatest aromatase activity survives the FSH decline it causes through estradiol and inhibin B. This is the **FSH threshold/window** concept (Brown; Baird). Antral follicles emerge in two to three waves per cycle (Baerwald and colleagues, ultrasound studies).

**Atresia** mainly proceeds by granulosa apoptosis (Tilly). Autophagy and other death modes are increasingly described.

**Controversy.** The dogma of a fixed, non-renewing reserve was challenged by Johnson and Tilly (2004), who claimed postnatal oogonial stem cells. Lineage-tracing work (Lei & Spradling 2013; Zhang and colleagues) found no meaningful contribution, and most investigators still reject renewal.
levels.expert:
**Clinical reading of the reserve.** Serum **AMH** comes from granulosa cells of small growing preantral and antral follicles. It correlates with antral follicle count and predicts response to ovarian stimulation. It does not reliably predict natural fecundability or the exact timing of menopause. Pitfalls include values suppressed by hormonal contraception, falsely low results after recent pregnancy, and differences between assays.

**Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)** is the commonest endocrine disorder of reproductive-age women. Its histology shows a thickened, collagenized tunica albuginea and many subcapsular antral follicles arrested at roughly 2 to 9 mm. The theca interna is hyperplastic and luteinized, and the stroma is hyperthecotic. Excess thecal androgen, high AMH and insulin resistance together stall dominance. The Rotterdam criteria accept polycystic morphology as one element, and AMH is gaining traction as a surrogate. Stromal hyperthecosis in postmenopausal women can resemble PCOS histologically.

**Iatrogenic and genetic insufficiency.** Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide deplete the primordial pool. One proposed mechanism is direct DNA damage to oocytes through **TAp63**-mediated apoptosis. Another is the "burnout" hypothesis of excess PI3K activation, which remains contested. Fertility preservation options include oocyte or embryo cryopreservation and **ovarian cortex cryopreservation** with later autotransplant, which has produced many live births. **In vitro activation**, which disrupts Hippo signalling by fragmenting the cortex and adds PI3K stimulators (Kawamura and colleagues, 2013), has yielded births in primary ovarian insufficiency, though its efficacy is debated. Genetic causes of premature ovarian insufficiency include **FMR1 premutation**, Turner syndrome with accelerated germ-cell loss, and variants in BMP15, GDF9 and NOBOX.

**Neoplasia mapped to histology.** Ovarian tumours follow the cell types seen on the slide:
- **Sex cord-stromal tumours**: adult granulosa cell tumour, defined by a FOXL2 C134W mutation, with Call-Exner bodies and coffee-bean nuclei. Thecomas and Sertoli-Leydig tumours (DICER1) also belong here.
- **Germ cell tumours**: teratoma and dysgerminoma.
- **Epithelial tumours**: many high-grade serous carcinomas actually arise in the fallopian tube fimbriae (serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma, STIC), not the surface epithelium. This finding reshaped prevention toward salpingectomy.

**Frontiers.** Researchers are mapping follicles with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics and growing follicles in 3D engineered matrices ("artificial ovary"). In mice, oocytes have been derived in vitro from pluripotent stem cells (Hayashi and Saitou). Open questions include what selects the dominant follicle beyond FSH sensitivity, and whether ovarian ageing is primarily oocyte-intrinsic or stromal, for example through stromal fibrosis and inflammaging.

keyPoints: Ovary: surface epithelium, tunica albuginea, follicle-rich cortex, vascular medulla
Follicle stages: primordial, primary, secondary (antral), Graafian
Oocytes arrest in prophase I until the LH surge, then at metaphase II until fertilization
Two-cell model: theca makes androgens (LH), granulosa aromatizes them to estradiol (FSH)
After ovulation the corpus luteum makes progesterone, then becomes the corpus albicans
Over 99% of follicles undergo atresia; AMH reflects the growing follicle pool

test.q: Which follicle stage has an oocyte surrounded by a single layer of flat cells?
test.explain: Primordial follicles have one layer of squamous pregranulosa cells. In primary follicles these cells become cuboidal.

test.q: The glycoprotein coat that forms around the oocyte in primary follicles is the:
test.explain: The zona pellucida (ZP1-ZP4) appears in the primary follicle, between the oocyte and the granulosa cells.

test.q: In the two-cell model, which cells convert androgens to estradiol?
test.explain: FSH induces aromatase in granulosa cells. Theca interna cells make the androgen precursors under LH.

test.q: At what stage is the oocyte arrested inside a primordial follicle?
test.explain: Primary oocytes stay arrested in prophase I (diplotene) until the LH surge. Metaphase II is the arrest after ovulation.

test.q: The granulosa cells that directly surround the zona of an ovulated egg form the:
test.explain: The corona radiata is the innermost layer of cumulus granulosa cells, and it travels with the egg.

test.q: What does the corpus luteum mainly secrete?
test.explain: Granulosa lutein cells produce large amounts of progesterone, which prepares the uterus for pregnancy.

test.q: If pregnancy occurs, which hormone rescues the corpus luteum?
test.explain: hCG from the early embryo acts like LH and keeps the corpus luteum alive.

test.q: Most ovarian follicles end their life through:
test.explain: More than 99% of follicles undergo atresia. Only about 400 are ever ovulated.

test.q: Small fluid spaces among granulosa cells that coalesce into the antrum are called:
test.explain: Call-Exner bodies are small fluid pockets in the granulosa. They later merge into the antrum.

test.q: A regressed corpus luteum becomes a white scar called the corpus ___.
test.explain: Corpus albicans means 'white body', a hyalinized scar.

test.q: What is the large fluid-filled cavity of a mature follicle called?
test.explain: The antrum defines secondary and Graafian follicles.

test.q: The mature follicle is also called the ___ follicle.
test.explain: It is named after Regnier de Graaf.

kidTest.q: What is a follicle?
choices: A cluster of cells around an egg
A small bone deep inside the hip joint
A flat muscle wall across the lower belly
kidTest.explain: A follicle is the egg plus the helper cells around it.

kidTest.q: About how big is an ovary?
kidTest.explain: Each ovary is roughly almond-sized.

kidTest.q: What is it called when a follicle lets its egg out?
kidTest.explain: Ovulation is the release of the egg.

kidTest.q: What does the leftover nest do after the egg leaves?
kidTest.explain: It turns yellow and makes hormones.

kidTest.q: The organ that holds the eggs is the o _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Ovaries store and release eggs.

advancedTest.q: Oocyte-specific Pten deletion in mice causes premature ovarian insufficiency mainly because:
choices: The whole primordial pool activates at once and is depleted
Granulosa cells lose aromatase and stop making estradiol
Oocytes fail to form a zona pellucida at the primary stage
The LH surge no longer restarts meiosis in the oocyte
advancedTest.explain: PTEN restrains PI3K/AKT. Without it, all primordial follicles activate and the reserve burns out early.

advancedTest.q: LH receptors are not on the oocyte. How does the LH surge still restart meiosis?
choices: Estradiol from theca cells directly activates oocyte MPF
Falling cGMP reaches the oocyte, freeing PDE3A to lower cAMP
Progesterone from the corpus luteum triggers vesicle breakdown
LH crosses the zona and binds oocyte nuclear receptors
advancedTest.explain: LH lowers NPPC/NPR2 signalling and closes gap junctions. Less cGMP reaches the oocyte, so PDE3A becomes active and cAMP falls.

advancedTest.q: Why does the dominant follicle survive while its cohort becomes atretic?
choices: It ovulates before the other follicles have formed an antrum yet
It has LH receptors and aromatase, so it tolerates falling FSH
It makes the most AMH, which blocks the FSH action on its rivals
It lacks theca cells, so it escapes androgen-driven atresia early
advancedTest.explain: Estradiol and inhibin B lower FSH. The follicle that is most sensitive and has LH receptors stays above its threshold.

advancedTest.q: Why did the STIC discovery shift ovarian cancer prevention toward salpingectomy?
choices: Granulosa cell tumours mostly arise in the tubal wall
Many serous carcinomas seem to begin in the tube fimbriae
AMH from the tube drives growth of ovarian surface cells
Teratomas form from germ cells stored in the tubes
advancedTest.explain: Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma in the fimbriae is a likely origin of many high-grade serous cancers, so removing the tubes may prevent them.

lessons.title: Uterus, Placenta & Breast

levels.kid:
Inside a woman's belly is the **uterus**, a strong, stretchy bag made mostly of muscle. Its inside lining is like a soft, cozy bed. Every month the bed gets thicker, just in case a baby starts to grow. If no baby comes, the old bed is shed and a new one is built.

If a baby does start to grow, a special organ called the **placenta** forms. It is like a busy trading post. Food and oxygen pass from mom's blood to the baby, and waste goes back. The two bloods stay separated by a very thin wall.

After the baby is born, the **breasts** make milk. Under the microscope they look like bunches of tiny grapes, each grape a little milk factory.
levels.hs:
The **uterus** has three layers. The inner **endometrium** is a lining of simple columnar epithelium with glands, sitting on a cell-rich connective tissue called the **stroma**. The thick middle **myometrium** is smooth muscle. The outer layer is the **perimetrium**, a covering membrane.

The endometrium has two zones:
- The **functional layer** (stratum functionalis) thickens each cycle and is shed during menstruation.
- The **basal layer** (stratum basalis) stays put and regrows the functional layer.

In the **proliferative phase**, the hormone **estrogen** makes glands grow straight and long. After ovulation, **progesterone** drives the **secretory phase**: glands become coiled and full of nutrients. When hormone levels fall, the **spiral arteries** constrict, the functional layer dies, and menstruation begins.

The **placenta** joins mother and fetus. Fetal tissue forms branching **chorionic villi** that float in pools of maternal blood. Each villus is covered by **trophoblast** cells and contains fetal capillaries. Oxygen and nutrients cross this thin barrier, but the two blood supplies do not normally mix.

The **mammary gland** is a modified sweat gland. Milk is made in small sacs called **alveoli** and flows through ducts to the nipple. A real example: during pregnancy, the breast changes dramatically. Its alveoli multiply so that the gland is ready to produce milk after birth.
levels.college:
**Uterus.** The wall consists of endometrium, myometrium, and perimetrium (serosa) or adventitia.
- **Endometrium**: simple columnar epithelium, with ciliated and secretory cells, over a cellular stroma. It contains tubular glands and **spiral arteries**, which branch from basal (straight) arteries. The straight arteries supply only the stratum basalis, so the basalis survives menstruation.
- **Proliferative phase** (estrogen): the epithelium regenerates and the glands are straight and narrow with mitoses.
- **Secretory phase** (progesterone): subnuclear glycogen vacuoles appear first (early secretory). The glands then become sawtooth and secretory, the stroma becomes edematous, and stromal cells become **predecidual**.
- **Menstrual phase**: falling progesterone causes spiral artery vasoconstriction, ischemia, and shedding of the functionalis.
- **Myometrium**: interlacing smooth muscle bundles. In pregnancy these undergo hypertrophy and hyperplasia and gain gap junctions (connexin 43) before labor.
- The **cervix** is dense collagenous tissue with mucus-secreting endocervical glands. Its ectocervix is nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. These two epithelia meet at the **transformation zone**.

**Placenta.** The placenta is **hemochorial**: maternal blood directly bathes fetal trophoblast.
- **Syncytiotrophoblast**: a multinucleated outer layer that secretes **hCG**, progesterone, and human placental lactogen.
- **Cytotrophoblast**: inner stem cells that become sparse in later pregnancy, which thins the barrier.
- The villus core holds fetal capillaries and **Hofbauer cells** (fetal macrophages).
- On the maternal side, stromal cells become **decidual cells**: large, pale, and glycogen-rich.

**Breast.** The breast is a compound tubuloalveolar gland of 15 to 20 lobes. Its functional unit is the **terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU)**. Ducts and alveoli have two cell layers: luminal secretory cells and **myoepithelial** cells. Proteins are released by exocytosis, while lipid leaves by **apocrine** secretion. **Prolactin** drives milk synthesis, and **oxytocin** contracts the myoepithelial cells.
levels.phd:
**Endometrial cycling as a model of scarless regeneration.** The human endometrium undergoes roughly 400 cycles of shedding and repair in a lifetime without scarring. Candidate regenerative populations include SSEA-1+/SOX9+ basalis epithelial progenitors and **perivascular mesenchymal stem cells** (CD140b+CD146+, and SUSD2+ cells). **Decidualization** of stromal fibroblasts is driven by progesterone acting with cAMP signaling through PRL, IGFBP1, FOXO1 and HAND2. Unusually in mammals, it is spontaneous in humans, occurring each cycle whether or not a pregnancy has begun. This matters because menstruation may be a consequence of spontaneous decidualization: progesterone withdrawal triggers an inflammatory cascade (prostaglandins, MMPs, leukocyte influx) and spiral arteriole constriction. Dating endometrium by histology (Noyes criteria, 1950) has poor reproducibility and little predictive value for fertility. This was shown by Coutifaris and colleagues in 2004, and the method has largely been abandoned for infertility work.

**Placentation.** Human placentation is **hemomonochorial** at term, with a single syncytial layer. The syncytium is maintained by continuous fusion of cytotrophoblasts. This fusion is mediated by **syncytin-1**, a co-opted endogenous retroviral envelope protein (HERV-W), acting through its receptor ASCT2. **Extravillous trophoblast** invades the decidua and remodels the spiral arteries. It replaces their smooth muscle and endothelium, converting them into dilated, low-resistance conduits. Decidual **uterine NK cells** (CD56bright, KIR-expressing) help control this. They interact with trophoblast HLA-C, HLA-E and HLA-G; trophoblast lacks classical HLA-A and HLA-B. Shallow remodeling is linked to preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. In preeclampsia, the soluble anti-angiogenic factor sFlt-1 is elevated. Early in the first trimester, trophoblast plugs block the spiral arteries, so the intervillous space is relatively hypoxic. Most researchers now regard this hypoxia as protective rather than pathological.

**Mammary gland.** Most mammary development happens after birth. At puberty, estrogen/ER and amphiregulin/EGFR signaling drive terminal end bud ductal elongation. During pregnancy, progesterone/RANKL and prolactin/JAK2-STAT5 signaling drive alveologenesis, with ELF5 specifying the luminal alveolar fate. In mice, lineage tracing (Van Keymeulen 2011) showed that luminal and basal lineages are largely maintained by unipotent progenitors after birth. This contradicted transplantation assays that had suggested bipotent stem cells. The disagreement shows how much the result depends on the assay. After weaning, involution remodels the gland by a STAT3-driven, lysosome-mediated cell death.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic pitfalls in the endometrium.** The **Arias-Stella reaction** occurs in pregnancy, including ectopic pregnancy. It produces hypersecretory glands with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei that can mimic clear cell carcinoma. Clues to the benign diagnosis are the clinical context and low proliferation. Finding only decidua and Arias-Stella change in a uterine sample, with no chorionic villi, should raise concern for **ectopic pregnancy**. Exogenous progestins produce a striking picture: atrophic glands within a decidualized stroma. Atypical hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, EIN) is diagnosed by architecture, with glands crowding out the stroma, and by cytologic change. Loss of PTEN or PAX2 on immunohistochemistry supports the diagnosis. Endometrial cancer is now classified molecularly following TCGA (2013) into four groups:
- POLE-ultramutated, with an excellent prognosis
- mismatch repair-deficient (MMRd), which prompts Lynch syndrome screening and makes the tumor a candidate for checkpoint inhibitors
- p53-abnormal, with a poor prognosis
- no specific molecular profile (NSMP)

This classification is now part of FIGO 2023 staging.

**Placental pathology.** Under the Amsterdam consensus terminology, lesions are grouped as **maternal vascular malperfusion** or **fetal vascular malperfusion**. Maternal vascular malperfusion includes infarcts, distal villous hypoplasia, accelerated villous maturation, and decidual arteriopathy with fibrinoid necrosis and foamy macrophages. **Villitis of unknown etiology** is a maternal T-cell attack on villi and tends to recur. Chorioamnionitis is graded by maternal and fetal inflammatory responses. Molar pregnancy is assessed with **p57** immunostaining. p57 is paternally imprinted, meaning only the maternal copy is expressed. It is therefore absent in complete moles, which are androgenetic, and retained in partial moles, which are triploid. **Placenta accreta spectrum** means villi attach to or invade the myometrium without intervening decidua. It is rising with cesarean scars and is a major cause of hemorrhage.

**Breast.** Most benign and malignant breast lesions arise in the TDLU. Myoepithelial markers (p63, SMMHC, calponin) separate in situ disease, where the myoepithelial layer is preserved, from invasive carcinoma. Tubular carcinoma and microglandular adenosis are notable exceptions. Loss of **E-cadherin** defines lobular carcinoma, giving its discohesive single-file pattern. Receptor and genomic profiling (ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67, and 21-gene or 70-gene assays) now guide therapy. HER2-low status has become actionable since antibody-drug conjugates were introduced.

**Open questions.** Several problems remain unresolved:
- Whether endometrial stem cells seed **endometriosis** by retrograde menstruation
- The origin of preeclampsia, where angiogenic ratio tests are reshaping triage
- Why the breast cancer risk added by pregnancy is transient, while early pregnancy protects against cancer over the long term

keyPoints: Uterine wall: endometrium, myometrium (smooth muscle), perimetrium
Functional endometrial layer sheds; basal layer regenerates it
Estrogen = proliferative (straight glands); progesterone = secretory (coiled glands)
Placental villi: syncytiotrophoblast + cytotrophoblast over fetal capillaries
Human placenta is hemochorial; maternal and fetal blood normally do not mix
Breast alveoli have luminal secretory cells plus contractile myoepithelial cells

p57 marks syncytin activity, which is lost in complete moles
p57 is expressed from the maternal allele, which complete moles lack
Complete moles have lost their cytotrophoblast layer

Adult mice lacking a myoepithelial layer in their mammary ducts
Transplants reveal potential that lineage tracing shows is unused
ELF5 specifying the basal lineage rather than the luminal alveolar one

lessons.title: The Eye: Cornea, Lens & Retinal Layers

levels.kid:
Your eye works a bit like a camera. At the front is the **cornea**, a clear window. It is so clear because it has no blood vessels in it at all.

Behind it sits the **lens**, like a soft, see-through jelly bean. The lens bends light so it lands in focus at the back of the eye.

The back of the eye is lined with the **retina**, a thin sheet of cells stacked in layers, like a cake. Special cells called **rods** and **cones** catch the light. Rods help you see in the dark. Cones help you see colors.

The retina then sends messages down the optic nerve to your brain, which turns them into pictures.
levels.hs:
Under the microscope, the eye shows how tissue structure serves function.

The **cornea** is the clear front of the eye. It has five layers:
- an outer **epithelium** (stratified squamous, not keratinized)
- **Bowman's layer**
- a thick **stroma** of collagen
- **Descemet's membrane**
- an inner **endothelium**, a single layer of cells

The cornea is **avascular**, meaning it has no blood vessels. It gets oxygen from the air and nutrients from the fluid behind it.

The **lens** is built of long, clear cells called **lens fibers**. They lose their nuclei and fill with proteins called **crystallins**. An elastic **capsule** surrounds the lens. Changing the lens's shape lets the eye focus near or far.

The **retina** is actually part of the brain that grew outward during development. It has 10 layers. Light passes through most of them before reaching the **photoreceptors** (rods and cones) at the back. Signals then travel forward through **bipolar cells** to **ganglion cells**, whose axons form the optic nerve.

A real example: the **fovea**, the spot you use for reading, contains only cones. The inner layers are pushed aside there, so light reaches the cones more directly.
levels.college:
**Cornea.** It provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power. Its layers, from front to back:
- **Epithelium**: stratified squamous and nonkeratinized, 5-7 cells thick. It is densely innervated, which is why the corneal reflex is so brisk. It is renewed from **limbal stem cells**.
- **Bowman's layer**: acellular collagen. It does not regenerate after injury.
- **Stroma**: about 90% of corneal thickness. It holds roughly 200 lamellae of type I collagen fibrils with uniform diameter and spacing, with sparse **keratocytes** between them. Proteoglycans such as keratan sulfate keep the spacing regular, and that regular spacing is the basis of transparency.
- **Descemet's membrane**: the thick basement membrane of the endothelium.
- **Endothelium**: a simple squamous layer. Its Na+/K+-ATPase and bicarbonate pumps keep the stroma dehydrated.

**Lens.** The capsule is a thick basement membrane. Under the anterior capsule lies a simple cuboidal **lens epithelium**. At the equator these cells elongate into **lens fibers**. Fibers lose their organelles, pack with α-, β- and γ-**crystallins**, and are added in layers throughout life. The lens hangs from **zonular fibers** attached to the ciliary body.

**Retina (outer to inner).**
1. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)
2. Photoreceptor layer (outer and inner segments)
3. Outer limiting membrane, formed by Müller cell junctions
4. Outer nuclear layer (photoreceptor nuclei)
5. Outer plexiform layer (photoreceptor-bipolar synapses)
6. Inner nuclear layer (bipolar, horizontal, amacrine and Müller cell nuclei)
7. Inner plexiform layer
8. Ganglion cell layer
9. Nerve fiber layer
10. Inner limiting membrane

The **RPE** phagocytoses shed outer-segment discs and recycles retinal for the visual cycle. **Müller glia** span the full thickness of the retina. At the optic disc there are no photoreceptors, which creates the blind spot.
levels.phd:
**Corneal transparency.** Maurice (1957) proposed that the stromal collagen fibrils, about 31 nm across, form a quasi-lattice that cancels scattered light by destructive interference. Benedek later showed that short-range order is enough, as long as the fibril spacing is smaller than the wavelength of light. Proteoglycans control both fibril diameter and spacing. Lumican knockout mice develop cloudy corneas, and mutations in keratan sulfate sulfotransferase (*CHST6*) cause macular corneal dystrophy. Stromal hydration is held at about 78% by the endothelial "pump-leak" balance. Human corneal endothelial cells barely divide, so lost cells are replaced by neighbors spreading out and enlarging. When cell density falls too far, the stroma swells with fluid (corneal edema).

**Lens.** Fiber cells break down their organelles through an organized, autophagy-like process. Phospholipase PLAAT3 has been implicated in breaking down organelle membranes. Clearing organelles removes structures that would scatter light. Crystallins are packed at an extraordinarily high concentration, among the highest protein concentrations of any tissue, and γ-crystallins are among the longest-lived proteins in the body. Their short-range packing, together with α-crystallin acting as a small heat-shock chaperone, prevents scattering. As crystallins age and accumulate damage, they aggregate and form cataracts. The lens has no blood supply, so ions and metabolites move through gap junctions (Cx46/Cx50) in an internal microcirculation.

**Retina.** The photoreceptor layer has a dense **interphotoreceptor matrix**. A rod outer segment holds about 1,000 discs stacked with rhodopsin. Discs are renewed constantly: Young's autoradiography studies (1967) showed new discs forming at the base and old discs moving toward the tip. Their tips are shed each morning and phagocytosed by the RPE through MERTK. The RPE also performs the canonical visual cycle, in which RPE65 isomerizes all-trans-retinyl esters into 11-cis-retinol. Cone pigments also draw on a second, Müller-glia-based cycle.

Retinal blood supply is split. The central retinal artery feeds the inner retina, while the choriocapillaris, through Bruch's membrane, feeds the outer retina. The fovea has neither inner vessels nor rods (the foveal avascular zone), so it depends entirely on the choroid.
levels.expert:
**Clinical histopathology.**
- **Endothelial keratoplasty.** DMEK transplants only Descemet's membrane and endothelium, using the layer structure as a surgical plane. Fuchs dystrophy shows **guttae**, collagen bumps on a thickened Descemet's membrane. It is commonly linked to a *TCF4* CTG repeat expansion that causes RNA toxicity.
- **Limbal stem cell deficiency** (for example after chemical burns) lets conjunctival epithelium with goblet cells grow over the cornea. Cultured limbal epithelial grafts (Holoclar) are an approved regenerative therapy.
- **Posterior capsule opacification** after cataract surgery comes from residual lens epithelial cells undergoing epithelial-mesenchymal transition and migrating over the capsule.
- **Retinal detachment** separates the neural retina from the RPE along the potential space left from the embryonic optic vesicle. This shows why the RPE-photoreceptor interface is held mainly by matrix and active RPE pumping rather than junctions.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** The optic nerve is CNS tract, myelinated by oligodendrocytes and wrapped in meninges. Papilledema reflects raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath, which blocks axoplasmic flow at the lamina cribrosa. **OCT** (optical coherence tomography) shows the retinal layers in living patients at near-histological resolution. Thinning of the ganglion cell and nerve fiber layers tracks pituitary-tumor compression of the chiasm and multiple sclerosis, and helps predict visual recovery after decompression.

**Pharmacology and toxicity.** Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy damages photoreceptors and RPE around the macula (a parafoveal ring in many patients, often more pericentral in Asian patients). Screening uses OCT and visual fields. Vigabatrin causes concentric field loss. Systemic corticosteroids promote posterior subcapsular cataract. Anti-VEGF agents treat choroidal neovascularization that breaks through Bruch's membrane.

**Frontier.** Voretigene neparvovec, a subretinal AAV2 gene therapy delivering *RPE65*, was the first FDA-approved gene therapy for an inherited disease (2017). Other active areas include optogenetic restoration of vision in ganglion cells, Müller glia reprogramming (which happens naturally in zebrafish), and transplanting stem-cell-derived RPE patches.

**Open questions** include why the macula is uniquely vulnerable in age-related macular degeneration (complement factor H variants and drusen beneath the RPE), and whether lens fiber organelle clearance can be modulated.

keyPoints: The cornea has 5 layers and is avascular; its transparency depends on uniformly spaced stromal collagen
The corneal endothelium pumps fluid out to keep the stroma dehydrated
Lens fibers lose their organelles and fill with crystallins; damaged crystallins aggregate into cataracts
The retina has 10 layers; light passes through the inner layers to reach the photoreceptors
The RPE phagocytoses shed outer-segment discs and recycles retinal (via RPE65)
The fovea has only cones, no inner retinal vessels, and depends on the choroid

test.q: What type of epithelium covers the front of the cornea?
test.explain: The corneal epithelium is stratified squamous and nonkeratinized, so it stays transparent. Skin epithelium is the keratinized type.

test.q: Which corneal layer keeps the stroma dehydrated by pumping?
test.explain: The endothelium's Na+/K+-ATPase and bicarbonate pumps move fluid out of the stroma. Descemet's membrane is only its basement membrane.

test.q: What makes up about 90% of corneal thickness?
test.explain: The stroma, made of collagen lamellae, makes up about 90% of the cornea's thickness.

test.q: Lens fibers become transparent mainly because they:
choices: Lose organelles and fill with crystallins
test.explain: Removing organelles eliminates structures that scatter light, and tightly packed crystallins keep the cytoplasm clear.

test.q: Where do new lens fibers form?
test.explain: Lens epithelial cells elongate into fibers at the equator, adding new layers throughout life.

test.q: In the retina, which layer contains photoreceptor nuclei?
test.explain: Rod and cone nuclei sit in the outer nuclear layer. Bipolar cell nuclei are in the inner nuclear layer.

test.q: Which cells phagocytose shed outer-segment discs?
test.explain: The RPE ingests the disc tips that photoreceptors shed each day and recycles retinal.

test.q: Why is the optic disc a blind spot?
choices: It is covered by thick pigment
test.explain: Ganglion cell axons exit the eye at the optic disc, so there are no photoreceptors there to detect light.

test.q: Which glial cells span the full thickness of the retina?
test.explain: Müller glia run from the inner to the outer limiting membrane. Their junctions form the outer limiting membrane.

test.q: What are the transparent proteins that fill lens fibers called?
test.explain: α-, β- and γ-crystallins are packed densely in lens fibers, and their regular packing keeps the lens clear.

test.q: The cornea has no blood vessels, so it is described as ___.
test.explain: Being avascular helps the cornea stay clear. It gets oxygen from the air and nutrients from the aqueous humor.

test.q: The ___ is the retinal pit used for sharp reading vision and contains only cones.
test.explain: At the fovea the inner layers are pushed aside, so light reaches the densely packed cones more directly.

kidTest.q: What is the cornea?
choices: A colored ring in the eye
A clear window at the front
kidTest.explain: The cornea is the clear window at the front of the eye.

kidTest.q: What does the lens do?
choices: It sends messages to the brain
kidTest.explain: The lens bends light so it lands in focus at the back of the eye.

kidTest.q: Which cells help you see colors?
kidTest.explain: Cones help you see colors. Rods help you see in the dark.

kidTest.q: How does the eye send pictures to the brain?
kidTest.explain: The retina sends its signals to the brain along the optic nerve.

kidTest.q: The layer of light-catching cells at the back of the eye is the r _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The retina is a layered sheet that contains the rods and cones.

advancedTest.q: Corneal stroma swells after endothelial cell loss. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Bowman's layer regenerates too quickly and traps fluid in the stroma
Limbal stem cells overproduce epithelium that blocks oxygen entry
The pump-leak balance fails because the endothelium barely divides
Keratocytes convert their collagen to type III scar tissue
advancedTest.explain: Human corneal endothelium has little capacity to divide. When cell density falls too far, pumping can no longer offset fluid leaking in, and the stroma becomes edematous.

advancedTest.q: A lesion of the central retinal artery mainly spares which layer, and why?
choices: The photoreceptors, because the choriocapillaris supplies them
The inner nuclear layer, because the RPE supplies it
The ganglion cells, because the choroid supplies them
The nerve fiber layer, because the vitreous nourishes it
advancedTest.explain: The central retinal artery feeds the inner retina. The outer retina, including the photoreceptors, is supplied from the choriocapillaris through Bruch's membrane.

advancedTest.q: Young's autoradiography in rods showed labeled protein moving from the base of the outer segment toward its tip. This implies:
choices: Discs are assembled at the tip and resorbed at the base
Discs are renewed at the base and shed at the tip for RPE uptake
Outer segments are fixed structures formed in the embryo
Rhodopsin diffuses freely between neighboring disc membranes
advancedTest.explain: New discs form at the base and move toward the tip, where the oldest discs are shed and phagocytosed by the RPE.

advancedTest.q: Retinal detachment usually separates the neural retina from the RPE. What histology underlies this?
choices: A weak point in Bruch's membrane lying under the choriocapillaris
Fragility of the inner limiting membrane overlying the fovea
Tight desmosomes that firmly join the RPE to the photoreceptor layer
A potential space from the optic vesicle, lacking junctions
advancedTest.explain: The neural retina and RPE come from the two layers of the embryonic optic cup. They are held together by matrix and RPE pumping rather than cell junctions, so they can separate along this plane.

lessons.title: Inner Ear: Cochlea & Vestibular Hair Cells

levels.kid:
Deep inside your head, behind each ear, is a tiny snail-shaped tube called the **cochlea**. It is full of liquid. When sound comes in, the liquid wiggles.

Inside the snail are special cells called **hair cells**. Each one has a little bundle of stiff "hairs" on top, lined up like organ pipes from short to tall. When the liquid wiggles, the hairs bend, and the cell sends a message to your brain: "Sound!"

Next to the snail are loops and little sacs that help with **balance**. They have hair cells too. When you spin or tip your head, the liquid moves and bends their hairs, so your brain knows which way is up.

Hair cells are precious. Very loud noise can break them, and people cannot grow new ones.
levels.hs:
The inner ear sits inside the hardest part of the skull, the **temporal bone**. It is a set of fluid-filled tubes called the **labyrinth**, and it has two jobs: hearing and balance.

**Hearing: the cochlea.** The cochlea is a spiral tube with about 2.5 turns. Cut across, it shows three fluid-filled channels. The middle one, the **cochlear duct**, holds the sensing structure, the **organ of Corti**. The organ of Corti rests on the **basilar membrane**. It has one row of **inner hair cells** and three rows of **outer hair cells**. A jelly-like flap, the **tectorial membrane**, lies over them.

Sound makes the basilar membrane vibrate. The hair cells' bundles of **stereocilia** are pressed against the tectorial membrane, so they bend. Bending opens ion channels, and the cell signals the **cochlear nerve**. Each place along the spiral is tuned to its own pitch. High pitches are sensed near the base and low pitches near the tip, called the **apex**.

**Balance: the vestibular system.** Three **semicircular canals** sense head rotation. Two sacs, the **utricle** and **saccule**, sense gravity and straight-line acceleration.

Real example: noise-induced hearing loss happens when loud sound damages hair cells. Mammals cannot regrow them, so the loss is permanent. This is why hearing protection matters.
levels.college:
**Labyrinth organization.** A bony labyrinth in the petrous temporal bone contains a membranous labyrinth. **Perilymph**, which resembles extracellular fluid (high Na+), surrounds the membranous labyrinth. **Endolymph**, unusually high in K+, fills it.

**Cochlear cross-section.** Three channels are visible:
- **Scala vestibuli** (perilymph), above **Reissner's (vestibular) membrane**
- **Scala media / cochlear duct** (endolymph)
- **Scala tympani** (perilymph), below the **basilar membrane**

The two perilymph scalae meet at the apex, the **helicotrema**. The **stria vascularis** lines the outer wall of the scala media. It is a rare vascularized epithelium that secretes K+ and produces the **endocochlear potential** of about +80 mV. The **spiral ganglion**, made of bipolar neurons, sits in the central bony core, the **modiolus**.

**Organ of Corti.**
- **Inner hair cells** (about 3,500 per cochlea) are flask-shaped and form one row. They are the true sensory transducers, and about 95% of afferent fibers (type I) contact them.
- **Outer hair cells** (about 12,000) are cylindrical and form three rows. They receive mainly efferent innervation from the olivocochlear bundle.
- **Supporting cells** include pillar cells, which enclose the tunnel of Corti, and Deiters' (phalangeal) cells.
- The tips of the tallest outer hair cell stereocilia are embedded in the **tectorial membrane**.

**Tonotopy.** At the base, the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff and responds to high frequencies. At the apex, it is wide and floppy and responds to low frequencies. Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

**Vestibular hair cells.** The **maculae** of the utricle and saccule carry an **otolithic membrane** loaded with calcium carbonate **otoconia**, which makes them sensitive to gravity. The **cristae ampullares** sit in the ampullae of the semicircular canals and are capped by a gelatinous **cupula**. Vestibular hair cells come in two types. **Type I** cells are flask-shaped and wrapped in an afferent calyx. **Type II** cells are cylindrical with bouton endings. Each vestibular bundle has one true **kinocilium** beside graded stereocilia. Mature cochlear hair cells lose their kinocilium.
levels.phd:
**Mechanotransduction.** Stereocilia are rigid, actin-filled projections arranged in a staircase. **Tip links** connect the tip of each shorter stereocilium to the side of its taller neighbor. Each tip link is built from **cadherin-23** (upper part) and **protocadherin-15** (lower part). The mechanotransduction (MET) channel sits at the lower end of the link. Its pore-forming subunits are **TMC1/TMC2**, with partners TMIE, LHFPL5 and CIB2.

Deflection toward the tallest row increases tension and opens the channels. Deflection the other way closes them. Gating is extremely fast (microseconds), which is too quick for a second-messenger system and implies direct mechanical gating (Corey and Hudspeth).

The driving force is unusually large. The +80 mV endocochlear potential combined with a resting potential of about −45 to −70 mV gives roughly 125–150 mV across the apical membrane. This drives K+ *into* the cell, so depolarization costs the hair cell little metabolic energy. The K+ then leaves through basolateral channels such as KCNQ4 and is recycled through supporting cells via **connexin-26** gap junctions back to the stria. GJB2 (connexin-26) mutations are the most common cause of inherited nonsyndromic deafness.

**Synapse.** Inner hair cells release glutamate at **ribbon synapses**. These are organized by RIBEYE and use **otoferlin** as a calcium sensor together with Cav1.3 channels. The arrangement allows sustained, graded release that is phase-locked to the sound wave.

**Cochlear amplifier.** Outer hair cells express **prestin** (SLC26A5), a motor protein in the lateral membrane that changes length with voltage. This **electromotility** feeds energy back into the basilar membrane. It sharpens tuning and adds about 40–60 dB of sensitivity. Békésy described the traveling wave in cadavers, where it was passive and broadly tuned. Later recordings from living cochleae revealed sharp, nonlinear tuning that the cochlear amplifier explains. **Otoacoustic emissions** (Kemp, 1978) are a by-product of this amplifier. Whether hair bundle motility also contributes in mammals remains debated.

**Vestibular coding.** Hair cells across each macula are polarized around a curving line called the **striola**, so every direction of head tilt is represented. The semicircular canals work as push-pull pairs on opposite sides of the head.
levels.expert:
**Clinical histopathology.** Damage tends to follow a set pattern. **Aminoglycosides** and **cisplatin** enter hair cells partly through MET channels and generate reactive oxygen species. They destroy outer hair cells first, beginning at the base, so high frequencies are lost first. Noise trauma typically produces a notch near 4 kHz.

Liberman and Kujawa's work on **cochlear synaptopathy** ("hidden hearing loss") showed that moderate noise can permanently destroy ribbon synapses even when thresholds recover. Spiral ganglion neurons are then lost slowly over time. Proving this in humans is hard because temporal bone samples and noninvasive biomarkers are limited. **Sodium thiosulfate** is now approved to reduce cisplatin ototoxicity in children.

**Diagnostics that map to histology:**
- **Absent otoacoustic emissions** suggest outer hair cell failure.
- **Auditory neuropathy** shows present emissions with an absent or abnormal auditory brainstem response. It points to inner hair cell, synapse or nerve pathology; otoferlin (OTOF) mutations are the classic cause.
- **Ménière's disease** shows endolymphatic hydrops at autopsy, and gadolinium-enhanced MRI can now show it in living patients.
- **BPPV** results from dislodged otoconia drifting into a semicircular canal, usually the posterior canal. It is corrected by repositioning maneuvers such as Epley's.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Vestibular schwannomas arise from Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve within the internal auditory canal. Preserving hearing during resection depends on protecting the cochlear nerve and its blood supply, the labyrinthine artery, an end artery. Intraoperative auditory brainstem response monitoring is used to guide this. **Cochlear implants** bypass missing hair cells by stimulating spiral ganglion neurons directly. Results therefore depend on how many of those neurons survive, and electrodes are placed along the tonotopic map.

**Frontiers.**
- **Gene therapy**: dual-AAV delivery of OTOF restored hearing in children in trials reported from 2024 (for example, the Shu/Chen group, Regeneron's DB-OTO and Akouos).
- **Regeneration**: birds and fish regrow hair cells from supporting cells. In mammals, forcing **Atoh1** expression or blocking Notch signaling produces immature hair-cell-like cells, but these rarely reach functional maturity. Clinical trials of the Notch inhibitor LY3056480 were disappointing.
- **Imaging**: optical coherence tomography vibrometry is revealing micromechanics inside the organ of Corti and is reshaping models of the cochlear amplifier.

**Pitfall on slides**: Reissner's membrane is extremely thin and the tectorial membrane often lifts off during fixation. These are artifacts and should not be mistaken for disease.

keyPoints: Cochlear duct (endolymph, high K+) lies between scala vestibuli and scala tympani
Organ of Corti: 1 row of inner hair cells (main afferent signal), 3 rows of outer hair cells (amplifier)
Stria vascularis creates the +80 mV endocochlear potential
Tip links open TMC1/2 channels when bundles bend toward the tallest stereocilia
Tonotopy: base senses high pitch, apex senses low pitch
Maculae (otoconia) sense gravity; cristae (cupula) sense head rotation

test.q: Which cochlear channel contains the organ of Corti?
test.explain: The organ of Corti sits in the scala media (cochlear duct), on the basilar membrane. The other two scalae contain perilymph.

test.q: What is unusual about endolymph?
test.explain: Endolymph has a high K+ concentration, which is unusual for an extracellular fluid. Perilymph resembles ordinary extracellular fluid and is high in Na+.

test.q: Which structure produces the endocochlear potential?
test.explain: The stria vascularis is a vascularized epithelium that secretes K+ and generates the endocochlear potential of about +80 mV.

test.q: Where along the cochlea are high-frequency sounds detected?
test.explain: The base of the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff, so it is tuned to high frequencies. The wide, floppy apex is tuned to low frequencies.

test.q: How many rows of outer hair cells does the organ of Corti have?
test.explain: There are three rows of outer hair cells and a single row of inner hair cells.

test.q: Most afferent fibers of the cochlear nerve contact which cells?
test.explain: About 95% of afferent (type I) fibers contact inner hair cells, which are the true sensory transducers. Outer hair cells mostly receive efferent fibers.

test.q: The cristae ampullares of the semicircular canals detect:
test.explain: Cristae, capped by a cupula, detect rotation of the head. The maculae, with their otoconia, detect gravity and linear acceleration.

test.q: The crystals that load the otolithic membrane are made of:
test.explain: Otoconia are calcium carbonate crystals. Their weight makes the maculae sensitive to gravity.

test.q: A mature vestibular hair bundle differs from a mature cochlear one by having a:
test.explain: Vestibular bundles keep one true kinocilium, while mature cochlear hair cells lose theirs. Both kinds of bundle have stereocilia and tip links.

test.q: The gelatinous membrane that lies over the hair cells of the organ of Corti is the ___ membrane.
test.explain: The tectorial membrane overlies the organ of Corti. The tips of the tallest outer hair cell stereocilia are embedded in it.

test.q: What is the snail-shaped hearing organ of the inner ear called?
test.explain: The cochlea is a spiral tube with about 2.5 turns that houses the organ of Corti.

test.q: The bipolar neurons of the cochlea sit in the spiral ___ inside the modiolus.
test.explain: The spiral ganglion lies in the modiolus, the central bony core of the cochlea.

kidTest.q: What shape is the cochlea?
kidTest.explain: The cochlea is a spiral tube shaped like a snail shell.

kidTest.q: What do hair cells have on top?
choices: Tiny round eyes that sense light
kidTest.explain: Hair cells have bundles of stiff hairs that bend when the liquid around them moves.

kidTest.q: Besides hearing, the inner ear helps you with:
kidTest.explain: The loops and sacs next to the cochlea help you keep your balance.

kidTest.q: What can break hair cells?
kidTest.explain: Very loud noise can damage hair cells, and people cannot grow new ones.

kidTest.q: The cochlea is full of l _ _ _ _ _ that wiggles when sound comes in.
kidTest.explain: Sound makes the liquid inside the cochlea move, and that bends the hairs.

advancedTest.q: Why does hair cell depolarization cost the cell little metabolic energy?
choices: Calcium release from internal stores triggers the response without any ion flow
Na+ enters from perilymph through fast gated channels in the apical stereocilia
K+ enters, driven by the endocochlear potential that the stria vascularis sets up
Chloride leaves the cell passively through prestin pores in the lateral membrane
advancedTest.explain: The +80 mV endolymph and the cell's negative resting potential drive K+ inward. The stria vascularis supplies the energy, so the hair cell does not have to pump it.

advancedTest.q: A patient has absent otoacoustic emissions but early thresholds suggest the inner hair cells are intact. Which cells are most likely failing?
choices: Spiral ganglion neurons in the modiolus
Cells of the stria vascularis outer wall
Type I vestibular hair cells in the cristae
Outer hair cells and their prestin-based motility
advancedTest.explain: Otoacoustic emissions are a by-product of outer hair cell electromotility. Losing them points to outer hair cell failure.

advancedTest.q: Present otoacoustic emissions with an absent auditory brainstem response in an infant with an OTOF mutation localizes the defect to:
choices: The inner hair cell ribbon synapse
advancedTest.explain: Intact emissions show the outer hair cells work. Otoferlin is the calcium sensor at the inner hair cell ribbon synapse, so release of signal to the nerve fails.

advancedTest.q: Why does aminoglycoside ototoxicity usually affect high frequencies first?
choices: Outer hair cells at the base are destroyed first
Inner hair cells at the apex take up more drug
The tectorial membrane detaches near the apex
Otoconia dissolve, affecting low tones last
advancedTest.explain: Damage begins with basal outer hair cells, and the base is tuned to high frequencies by tonotopy.
